extracted.intended_audience: mathematics and computer-science students and authors preparing mathematical exposition (papers, proofs, books, manuals)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, sentence-to-document level rules and recommendations for writing mathematics clearly and professionally (notation, proofs, punctuation, typography, organization, and audience-aware exposition). Originates from a Stanford technical writing minicourse for CS/mathematics students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate symbols in adjacent formulas by words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Consider s., q < p." Good: "Consider S_q, where q < p." Always put words between adjacent symbolic expressions so the reader can parse relationships across formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with a mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "z^n - a has n distinct zeroes." Good: "The polynomial x^n - a has n distinct zeroes." Spell out or rephrase so sentences start with words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using non-word symbol shorthands in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use shorthand symbols (e.g., contractions or coding-like shorthands) in place of words in exposition (except in logic-heavy work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace cryptic symbols with their corresponding words in standard prose to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead‑in to theorem/algorithm must be a complete sentence or end with a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "We now have the following" followed immediately by "Theorem." Better: "We can now prove the following result." The lead-in should motivate and connect to prior discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theorem statements self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained and not depend on assumptions only given in preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theorem references earlier assumptions, restate them or give a clear pointer so the theorem can be read independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' judiciously to avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'we' to avoid passive constructions, but only when 'we' genuinely means the author and reader together; avoid using 'I' unless the author's persona matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' for an inclusive dialogic tone; avoid using 'we' as a formal equivalent of 'I'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sentence rhythm and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a definite rhythm in sentences—read and revise for smooth flow and appropriate word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words and phrasing for cadence; sometimes alternate between noun and gerund forms (e.g., 'merge patterns' vs 'merging patterns') to preserve rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'that' when it aids parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't omit the word 'that' when it helps the reader parse the sentence; use 'assume that' or 'suppose that' unless another 'that' appears nearby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But avoid unnecessary padding like 'because of the fact that'. Also avoid awkward 'We have that x = y' — prefer 'We have x = y.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure; use parallelism when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid monotonous sentence openings and word repetition; however, use parallel constructions when describing parallel concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't repeat the same transitional words in succession; use parallel forms (e.g., 'Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'homework paper' style of listing formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t write a sequence of formulas without connecting commentary; tie concepts together with running exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide narrative or explanatory sentences between formulas to guide the reader through the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: State things twice in complementary ways and define variables on first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinforce definitions or important concepts by restating them in complementary ways; define all variables (at least informally) when first introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: give both an informal description and a formal definition; use examples to clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate the reader and keep reader knowledge foremost
rubrics_metrics.description: Always consider what the reader already knows and what they should expect next; provide motivation, especially for your own results, and avoid superlative praise of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing others' work, either let results speak for themselves or give reasons why they are interesting; when describing your own, be humble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write so sentences still make sense when formulas are skimmed
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers will skim formulas on first reading; ensure prose flows when formulas are abstracted away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences should be readable when complex formulas are mentally replaced with placeholders like 'blah'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation and avoid reusing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use the same notation for two different things and use consistent notation for the same object throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose index letters and typographic conventions (e.g., lowercase for elements, uppercase for sets) and stick to them; if you must restate an object, make the restatement explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize and manage subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive subscripting and subscripted subscripts; don't name elements unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer referring to unspecified elements as x and y rather than X_1, X_2 unless indexing is required; avoid awkward nested subscript notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas on their own line and number selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Put important formulas on their own line and assign numbers only to the important ones (not every displayed equation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a displayed formula will be referred to elsewhere, number it; avoid numbering trivial or local displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sentences are unambiguous left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct sentences so they are readable from left to right without temporary ambiguity that misleads the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions that force the reader to backtrack; place words appropriately to prevent misparsing ('Smith remarked...' vs syntax causing confusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out small numbers when used as adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out small numbers used as adjectives but use numerals when talking about numbers as themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'The method requires 2 passes.' Good: 'Method 2 is illustrated... it requires 17 passes.' Use numerals for counts and numbers-as-names; spell out when adjectives improve flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize labels like Theorem, Lemma, Algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal object names in titles: Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Algorithm 3, Method 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain this typographic convention for clarity in headings and cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow common small style maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to grammar and common stylistic maxims: avoid dangling participles, sentence fragments, pronoun-antecedent disagreement, unnecessary commas, and gratuitous split infinitives (use judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a grab-bag of small rules—apply them to improve clarity and correctness; some rules (e.g., split infinitives) can be broken when it aids meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch common misspellings and hyphenation changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to frequently misspelled words and note current trends in hyphenation (e.g., 'nonnegative', 'nonzero' are no longer hyphenated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spell-checkers and prefer contemporary spellings in the literature of your field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'that' over 'which' in restrictive clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'that' for restrictive clauses (no comma) and 'which' when preceded by a comma or preposition or used interrogatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Don't use commas which aren't necessary.' Good: 'Don't use commas that aren't necessary.' Also avoid confusion between 'less' and 'fewer'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate correctly around displayed equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with punctuation before and after displayed equations; many writers mistakenly insert colons or other marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the display completes a sentence, adjust punctuation accordingly; avoid unnecessary colons introducing displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the opening paragraph and first sentence your best
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph and especially the first sentence should be the strongest; a bad start discourages readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bland openings like 'An x is y.' Instead provide motivation or consequence: 'Quicksort is an important method... because...' Hook the reader early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow usual quotation-mark punctuation conventions; keep punctuation logical with parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas and periods go inside quotation marks by convention, but other punctuation stays outside unless part of the quotation. Parentheses' internal punctuation should stand alone logically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conventional (sometimes illogical) American placement for commas/periods inside quotes, but ensure parentheses/brackets are punctuated in a logically consistent way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long noun strings and unnecessary jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist long noun sequences used as adjectives and unnecessary jargon; prefer clarity and nonspecialist vocabulary when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example bad noun string: 'packet switched data communication network protocol problem'—rephrase for readability and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor and exclamation points sparingly and carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be effective when readers understand the technical point; exclamation points should be used only when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jokes that don't survive rereading; be cautious with exclamation points in scholarly writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate programming notation from mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish programming-language notation from mathematical notation in formal writing (e.g., use subscripts rather than p[r], and avoid '*' for multiplication in math papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt mathematical conventions when writing for mathematical audiences; reserve program-like notation for code snippets or manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear vocabulary for relationships (component vs element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose precise nouns to avoid confusion: e.g., call p_i a 'component' of p rather than merely calling everything an 'element'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinct words for distinct subsidiary relationships to prevent ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses usage and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: When using ellipses (e.g., (p_1, ..., p_n)), place commas before/after the dots when appropriate; dots level (baseline or mid-level) depends on surrounding symbols; ensure proper spacing so '...;' doesn't look odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow typographic conventions for ellipses and use TeX spacing rules when typesetting; check spacing around ellipses in formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mid-formula line breaks; use typesetting tools to prevent them
rubrics_metrics.description: Linebreaks in the middle of formulas are undesirable; use typesetting features (e.g., TeX) to control breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent awkward breaking of symbols; tie closely related tokens using nonbreaking constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meta-comments to signal proof strategies and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Include brief comments like 'We demonstrate the second conclusion by contradiction' or 'There must be a witness...' to tell the reader what's going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signposting helps the reader follow long proofs—use comments and named subgoals to show structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number displayed formulas only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Number only those displayed formulas that are important or will be referenced elsewhere; avoid numbering all displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraneous numbering distracts and clutters; reserve numbers for cross-reference targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous parentheses and nested parentheses when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove unnecessary parentheses and avoid nested parentheses unless required; when nested pairs are needed, typographers often use larger outer parentheses rather than switching to brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to reduce parentheses; if displaying a definition in formula (2) you may need to avoid an outer parenthesis altogether.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with typographic devices (fonts, boldface, quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse multiple fonts, boldface, or excessive quotation marks; too many typographic devices distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic emphasis only where it clarifies; limit the number of distinct styles in a single document.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-proof marking
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a box or 'Q.E.D.' at the end of a proof; if using a box, leave a space between it and the final period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent visual marker for proof termination; format so the box is visually distinct from sentence-ending punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraph boundaries clear when using displays
rubrics_metrics.description: When using displayed formulas, ensure it's clear where new paragraphs begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous breaks by providing lead-in or trailing text; consider paragraph indentation or an extra linebreak for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate notation conventions for audience (bold vectors, arrows, roman superscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notational or typographic conventions appropriate to readers (e.g., boldface or arrows for vectors); avoid confusing superscript formatting like 'i+st'—use roman type for 'i+st'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your conventions are standard for your intended audience and document them if nonstandard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychologically bad line breaks; use nonbreaking spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent awkward line breaks that separate final symbols from their sentence; when using TeX, use '~' to tie tokens across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check typeset output for orphan symbols or awkward breaks and correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spell checkers and minimize typos
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who are weak spellers should use spelling checkers to avoid needless errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell-checking is essential for professional-looking documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep formulas compact and use 'name-and-conquer' for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessively long formulas that are hard to format or understand; name subexpressions to simplify manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replace v = C + U(C_i - C_j + 1) with v = C + k_u where k = c_i - c_j + 1 when you repeatedly manipulate the subexpression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts and unnecessary indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer simpler variable names over heavy indexing; avoid naming elements unnecessarily (e.g., use p in P rather than p_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler notation improves readability, especially in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing symbolic sequences without connecting words; place words between adjacent formulas to explain operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: 'Add P k times to c.' Better: 'Add P to c k times.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before use or immediately nearby
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure symbols are defined before they are used or at least immediately adjacent to their first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should not have to search for definitions; place definitions close to usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence forms but use parallelism for related concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get stuck on repetitive sentence openings; however, enforce parallelism when discussing parallel notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical repetition of the same transition words; use variety for better flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sentences comprehensible left-to-right by naming conditions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange sentences so their logical subject and verb are predictable early; for conjunctive claims, name the conditions explicitly before stating the implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'We prove that (grunt) and (snort) implies (blah).' Better: 'We prove that the two conditions (grunt) and (snort) imply (blah).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in wording; don't conflate subtly different terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terminology precisely—e.g., 'not nonincreasing' is not the same as 'increasing'; choose words that reflect exact meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misstating logical or quantificational nuance confuses readers; prefer explicit phrasing where ambiguity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain tense consistency for a subject; either use present tense uniformly or use sequential (temporal) tenses in longer expositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two recommended approaches: (a) Use present tense throughout, or (b) write sequentially (e.g., 'We saw..., we will see...') for long papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs over proofs by contradiction when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid proofs by contradiction if a direct proof exists; direct proofs often yield clearer exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of supposing dependence and deriving contradiction, show coefficients must be zero directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a conversational tone with signposts and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give signposts and transition paragraphs to lead readers through complex arguments; a conversational tone often improves readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'The operative word is zero,' or 'We divide the proof into two parts...' help orient readers and break up dense technical text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose numeral vs. written form to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use digits or words appropriately to avoid ambiguity between numeral and pronoun senses (e.g., 'one' vs '1').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the context makes 'one' ambiguous, use the digit '1' for the numeral sense; similarly choose numerals for counts when clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on inclusive language conventions consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in choices like 'he', 'he or she', or singular 'they'; be aware readers' expectations and aim for unobtrusive solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different authorities disagree; choose a consistent policy that suits audience and publication standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material clearly; weave branches and threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization is crucial—present material in a way that threads alternate branches together rather than a flat linear list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on overall structure (plots) of exposition; good organization is recognizable even if hard to formalize—use outlines, transitions, and restructuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: When self-publishing, value professional copyeditors and designers
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in self-publishing contexts, the expertise of copy editors and book designers improves readability and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (page width, fonts, margins) affect readability; consider professional help for final drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation conventions and avoid over-sensitivity to minor choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Some punctuation choices (e.g., comma before 'that', 'then' after 'if') are stylistic; use them to enhance clarity and reading speed rather than dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including or omitting words like 'that' or 'then' improves parsing for your audience, prefer clarity over strict adherence to prescriptive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with coincident punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons)
rubrics_metrics.description: When punctuation marks coincide (e.g., comma and period), follow standard practice (write only the appropriate single mark); coincident commas are not inherently a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn conventional rules for resolving coincident marks; don't overreact to coincident punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything that helps communication is good; avoid what hurts communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching criterion: prefer any technique that improves clarity and avoid anything that distracts or confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This meta-rule permits breaking lesser rules when doing so improves communication; always evaluate stylistic choices by whether they aid reader comprehension.
